27:4.text: Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.

provenance.route: Philippians 2:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Leviticus 19:18's object substituted
provenance.other: “esteem other better” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Philippians 2:3, and it is the KJV's only use of ‘esteem’ to govern the regard of one member of a congregation for another. The object Mosiah gives it — ‘his neighbor as himself’ — is Leviticus 19:18's, which the KJV always attaches to ‘love’.
provenance.significance: The verse is a graft. Mosiah 27:4 takes the verb of Philippians 2:3 and the object of Leviticus 19:18 and makes a sentence neither has: ‘every man should esteem his neighbor as himself’. What that does is convert the second great commandment into a measurable standard of civic equality — the surrounding clauses are about pride, haughtiness and a levelled priesthood — because ‘love thy neighbour’ names an affection and ‘esteem’ names a valuation. Philippians 2:3's own subject is the same, a congregation ordered against strife and vainglory, and 2:4-8 goes on to ground it in Christ emptying himself; Mosiah grounds it instead in priests working with their own hands.

27:4.note: ‘That they should let no pride nor haughtiness disturb their peace; that every man should esteem his neighbor as himself.’ The prohibition matches Philippians 2:3's ‘strife or vainglory’ in function and the verb is that verse's alone in the KJV, but the object comes from the Levitical commandment. Filed high because the substitution is the argument: an ordinary writer reaching for Leviticus 19:18 reproduces ‘love’, and this one does not.

27:5.text: And labour, working with our own hands: being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it:

provenance.other: “with our own hands” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, and only 1 Corinthians 4:12 joins the phrase to labour as a minister's self-support; the other is Deuteronomy 32:27, of enemies boasting. The KJV's other self-support texts read ‘work with your own hands’ (1 Thessalonians 4:11) and ‘working with his hands’ (Ephesians 4:28).
provenance.significance: The clause Mosiah borrows is followed immediately in Paul by ‘being persecuted, we suffer it’ — and Mosiah 27 opens on persecution (27:1-3) and closes on it (27:32, ‘being greatly persecuted … being smitten by many of them’). So the chapter's frame and its economic rule come from the same sentence of 1 Corinthians 4. What Mosiah adds is a clause Paul never needed: ‘in all cases save it were in sickness, or in much want’, which turns an apostolic boast into an administrative exemption. That is this chapter's habit throughout — the New Testament supplies a posture and the Book of Mormon supplies the by-law.

27:5.note: ‘All their priests and teachers should labor with their own hands for their support.’ The pairing of labour with a possessed pair of hands is Pauline in three places and 1 Corinthians 4:12 is the one that has the possessive Mosiah has, the plural subject Mosiah has, and the persecution setting Mosiah 27 has. The verse before it, 27:4, applies the same rule to every man, which is why the recurrence is filed rather than a second link.

27:5.text: Therefore, as ye abound in every thing, in faith, and utterance, and knowledge, and in all diligence, and in your love to us, see that ye abound in this grace also.

provenance.other: “abound in this grace” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 8:7. The verb and the noun meet in only one other place, 2 Corinthians 9:8, ‘God is able to make all grace abound toward you’, where grace is the subject rather than the thing abounded in.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 8 is Paul's collection letter: the grace the Corinthians are to abound in is money for Jerusalem, and the argument runs from a congregation's material generosity to the grace of Christ who became poor. Mosiah 27:5 ends its own paragraph about material arrangements — priests supporting themselves, exceptions for the sick and the destitute — with ‘doing these things, they did abound in the grace of God’. The borrowing is exact in its subject matter, which is what recommends it: both texts use the phrase of a community whose grace is demonstrated by how it handles money and labour.
provenance.alternative: 2 Corinthians 9:8, which is the more familiar verse but has the wrong grammar.

27:5.note: ‘And doing these things, they did abound in the grace of God.’ A KJV singleton, in a verse about congregational finance, closing a Book of Mormon paragraph about congregational finance. Moderate rather than high because ‘abound’ and ‘grace’ are both ordinary and the sentence could be assembled without a source. Note that the exclusion register rejects this same KJV verse at Mosiah 26:38, where the n-gram-friendly ‘in all diligence’ pointed at it for no reason; the real contact with 2 Corinthians 8:7 in this book is here, one chapter later, and it is with a different phrase.

27:9.text: And on this manner did Absalom to all Israel that came to the king for judgment: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

provenance.other: “stole the hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 15:6. Hearts are hardened, turned, enticed and won elsewhere in the KJV, but stolen only by Absalom.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one heart-thief is a king's son who flatters his way into a following and rebels against his father. Mosiah 27:8-9 has just told us that this Alma is ‘called Alma, after his father’, that he is ‘a man of many words’ who ‘did speak much flattery to the people’, and that he goes about stealing away their hearts. Absalom's method in 2 Samuel 15:1-6 is exactly that — standing in the gate, telling every suitor his cause is good, kissing the men who bow to him. Recover the rest of the Absalom narrative and the borrowing carries a threat the chapter then declines to execute: Absalom's father prays against his son's counsel and weeps for him, and the son dies in his rebellion. Alma's father prays for his son (27:14) and the son is knocked down and raised. The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's story of a rebellion that could only end in a father's grief and given it the other ending.

27:9.note: ‘Stealing away the hearts of the people.’ One KJV verse contains the idiom and it belongs to the archetypal rebellious son, which is what Mosiah 27:8 has just gone out of its way to establish this Alma is — named for his father, working against his father's church. The flattery of 27:8 is Absalom's technique in 2 Samuel 15:2-4 and the phrase in 27:9 is Absalom's summary verse. Note too that ‘much flattery’ at 27:8 reuses the ‘flattering words’ of 26:6, so the chapter is carrying its predecessor's vocabulary as well as its own source.

27:10.text: For ye have heard of my conversation in time past in the Jews’ religion, how that beyond measure I persecuted the church of God, and wasted it:

provenance.other: “persecuted the church of God” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Galatians 1:13 and 1 Corinthians 15:9, and both are Paul on himself before Damascus. Galatians 1:23 supplies the verb Mosiah actually uses: ‘he which persecuted us in times past now preacheth the faith which once he destroyed.’
provenance.significance: Mosiah 27:10 has Alma ‘going about to destroy the church of God’ and 27:13 has the angel ask ‘why persecuteth thou the church of God?’ — the two verbs the KJV attaches to Saul's pre-conversion career, in the KJV's own object phrase, four verses apart. Galatians 1:23 is where they meet: persecuted, then destroyed, then preached. Mosiah 27 completes the same triad — destroys (10), is confronted (13), and by 27:32-35 is ‘publishing to all the people the things which they had heard and seen’ and repairing what he wrecked. Galatians 1:14, the ‘traditions of my fathers’ verse, is already the source behind Mosiah 26:1, so this chapter is the second stop in the same paragraph of Galatians.

27:10.note: ‘While he was going about to destroy the church of God … seeking to destroy the church.’ The object phrase is Paul's autobiographical formula and the verb is the one Galatians 1:23 pairs with it. What raises the link above vocabulary is that Mosiah 27 goes on to run the whole Galatians 1 sequence — destroyer, confronted by a revelation, preacher of the faith he destroyed — and that the immediately preceding chapter had already drawn on Galatians 1:14.

27:12.text: And they that were with me saw indeed the light, and were afraid; but they heard not the voice of him that spake to me.

provenance.route: Acts 22:9 (with Acts 9:7) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV gives the Damascus companions twice and inconsistently: at Acts 9:7 they stand speechless, ‘hearing a voice, but seeing no man’; at Acts 22:9 they see the light ‘but they heard not the voice of him that spake to me’. Mosiah 27:12 takes the Acts 22 side — they fell, and ‘understood not the words which he spake unto them’.
provenance.significance: The difference between Acts 9:7 and Acts 22:9 is the classic crux of the Damascus narratives, and Mosiah 27:12 resolves it in the direction Acts 22 does, then softens it further: the companions do not fail to hear, they fail to understand. That is the harmonizing reading — the voice was audible but not intelligible — which is how the two Acts accounts have long been reconciled. The Book of Mormon verse takes a side in a New Testament textual problem, and the side it takes is the one that makes both KJV verses true at once.

27:12.note: ‘They fell to the earth, and understood not the words which he spake unto them.’ The falling is Acts 9:4's, the not-perceiving is Acts 22:9's, and the substitution of understanding for hearing is the standard harmonization of the two. High confidence: the wording is not distinctive on its own — ‘fell to the earth’ occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses — but a Damascus-road scene that lands precisely on the point where the KJV's two accounts disagree is not doing so by accident.

27:13.text: And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?

provenance.route: Acts 9:4 (with Acts 26:16) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “why persecutest thou” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses — Acts 9:4, 22:7 and 26:14 — which are the three tellings of one event. The KJV asks the question nowhere else. ‘Arise, and stand forth’ is not a KJV phrase; Acts 26:16's ‘But rise, and stand upon thy feet’ is the same command in the third telling, and Acts 9:6's ‘Arise, and go into the city’ supplies the verb.
provenance.significance: Everything is transposed by one step. The heavenly voice names the persecutor twice in Acts and once here; it asks why he persecutes ‘me’ in Acts and ‘the church of God’ here; and the speaker is the Lord in Acts and an angel here, sent by a Lord who is then quoted at second hand — ‘For the Lord hath said, This is my church.’ The last of those is the substantive change. Acts 9:4 identifies the church with Christ so completely that persecuting it is persecuting him, and Mosiah 27:13 declines the identification and replaces it with a possessive claim, ‘This is my church, and I will establish it’, which is the same claim the voice made to Alma's father at 26:22. The Book of Mormon keeps the Damascus question and answers it institutionally.
provenance.alternative: Acts 22:7 or 26:14, the parallel tellings; 9:4 is named because Mosiah 27:12-13 also has the falling to the earth, which 26:14 shares but 22:7 words differently.

27:13.note: The chapter's anchor. A KJV question asked in three verses about one man is asked here of another, in the same words but for a different object, and the whole scene around it — the light, the falling, the companions who do not understand, the days of helplessness, the raising up to preach — is the Damascus narrative. The 1830 reading is worth keeping in view: it has ‘why persecuteth thou’, which is not the KJV's grammar, and 1920 corrected it to ‘persecutest’, which is. That is the direction of change CONVENTIONS §8 flags — a later edition moving the text back toward its source — and it means the first edition shows the borrowing slightly less exactly than the modern text does.

27:13.text: He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.

provenance.other: “the transgression of my people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 53:8, and Mosiah 27:13 reproduces the five words entire. Isaiah 53 is transcribed whole into this book at Mosiah 14, and 53:8 is Mosiah 14:8.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 53:8 makes the transgression of my people the reason the servant was stricken. Mosiah 27:13 makes it the one thing that can overthrow the church: ‘nothing shall overthrow it, save it is the transgression of my people.’ The phrase has been moved from a cause of atonement to a cause of institutional collapse, and the speaker is an angel addressing a man in the act of trying to overthrow that church from outside — the verse's point being that he cannot, and that only the members can. This is the second of the batch's Isaiah 53 borrowings routed through Abinadi's transcription: Mosiah 26:14 took ‘poured out his soul’ from 53:12, and this takes ‘the transgression of my people’ from 53:8.
provenance.alternative: Direct dependence on Isaiah 53:8; nothing in the wording distinguishes Isaiah 53:8 from Mosiah 14:8, which reproduces it. The route is argued from the book's own contents, not from the words.

27:13.note: A five-word KJV singleton inside the angel's speech, taken from the Isaiah chapter this book has already transcribed twelve chapters earlier and put to a use Isaiah does not have. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is short, ordinary in its components, and its new sense is remote from Isaiah's; what recommends it is the absolute rarity and the established channel — Abinadi's Isaiah 53 is demonstrably in this narrator's hands, and Alma is the character whose whole standing derives from having believed it.

27:14.text: Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.

provenance.other: “the knowledge of the truth” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses: 1 Timothy 2:4, 2 Timothy 3:7 and Hebrews 10:26. Only 1 Timothy 2:4 uses it of a destination God wills people to reach; the other two use it of people who never arrive or who sin after arriving.
provenance.significance: 1 Timothy 2:1-4 is the KJV's argument that intercessory prayer for others is good and acceptable because God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Mosiah 27:14 is an angel explaining that a father's intercessory prayer has been heard, ‘that thou mightest be brought to the knowledge of the truth’. The source verse is the warrant for the very practice the angel has come to vindicate, and the chapter ends by reporting that the converts brought ‘many to the knowledge of the truth’ (27:36) — the prayed-for man becomes the answer to other people's prayers.

27:14.note: The phrase is not rare enough by itself to settle a source, but only one of its three KJV occurrences is about God's will that people arrive at it, and that occurrence sits inside the KJV's chief defence of praying for other people — which is exactly what Mosiah 27:14 is about. Moderate: real contact, short phrase, no clause reproduced.

27:16.text: Only fear the LORD, and serve him in truth with all your heart: for consider how great things he hath done for you.

provenance.other: “how great things he hath done for” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 12:24, and Mosiah 27:16 reproduces all seven words. The other KJV form of the idiom, “how great things the Lord hath done”, also occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 5:19, and inserts the divine name where Mosiah has none.
provenance.alternative: Mark 5:19, the Gadarene demoniac's commission, which the ranked machine stream and the memory of 1 Nephi 7:11 both pull toward. It loses on two words: Mark has ‘the Lord’ inside the run and Mosiah does not, while 1 Samuel 12:24 matches the run exactly.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 12 is Samuel's farewell at the making of the monarchy, and the ‘great things’ he tells Israel to consider are enumerated a few verses earlier: the LORD ‘brought forth your fathers out of the land of Egypt’ (12:6-11), a recital of bondage and deliverance. Mosiah 27:16 issues the same command with the same content — ‘remember the captivity of thy fathers in the land of Helam, and in the land of Nephi … for they were in bondage, and he hath delivered them.’ The angel is not merely using a biblical idiom; he is using the one KJV verse where that idiom means precisely what he wants it to mean, in a chapter of the KJV about a people who have just asked for a king and must now be told what their national deliverance obliges. Mosiah 27 is a chapter about a king's sons and a high priest's son, and the KJV verse behind its central command is Samuel's warning to a nation about its kings.

27:16.note: ‘Remember how great things he hath done for them: for they were in bondage, and he hath delivered them.’ A seven-word run from a KJV singleton, and the source's own context is a recital of deliverance from bondage. Mark 5:19 is the more famous home of the idiom and was adjudicated at 1 Nephi 7:11, where the 1830 ‘how’ preserved a reading 1920 removed; that argument is not restated here, because the run at Mosiah 27:16 matches 1 Samuel 12:24 word for word and Mark only with an insertion. The row is filed at high confidence on the exact run and the coinciding subject matter.

27:22.text: To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me.

provenance.other: Acts 26:18 is the commission the risen Christ gives Paul in the third and fullest Damascus telling, and it is the only place in the KJV where opened eyes, a turn from darkness to light, and a rescue from Satan's power are one sentence.
provenance.significance: The chapter distributes Acts 26:18's four clauses across its second half. The priests pray ‘that the eyes of the people might be opened to see and know of the goodness and glory of God’ (27:22); Alma reports being taken out of ‘the darkest abyss’ into light (27:29); the enemy of God whose power he had served is named at 27:9; and the forgiveness and inheritance come at 27:24 and 27:26. Acts 26:18 is Paul's own summary of what his conversion was for, and Mosiah 27 uses it as the summary of what Alma's was for — but redirects the opened eyes from the future audience to the present congregation, who are watching.

27:22.note: Conceptual rather than verbal, and marked so. The argument is that the chapter is already demonstrably working from the Damascus narratives (27:12, 27:13) and that this verse and 27:29 take up the commission clause of the fullest of them, in its order. kjvSpecific ‘uncertain’ because no phrase here is distinctive enough to test against another English version.

27:25.text: Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again.

provenance.other: “born again” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses, John 3:3, 3:7 and 1 Peter 1:23. Only John 3:7 puts it after ‘Marvel not that’, which occurs in exactly 4 KJV verses and nowhere else with this predicate.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 27:25 keeps John 3:7's opening and its close and replaces its middle: ‘Marvel not that I said unto thee’ becomes ‘Marvel not that all mankind, yea, men, and women, all nations, kindreds, tongues and people, must be born again’. What has been inserted is the universalizing catalogue, which is Revelation's list of the redeemed, and what has been displaced is Nicodemus. John 3:7 is a rebuke to one man's incredulity; Mosiah 27:25 turns the same sentence into a doctrine about every human being. The rest of the paragraph then supplies John 3's other terms in order — born of God, changed, becoming his sons and daughters (John 1:12-13), new creatures, and the kingdom of God that John 3:5 says the unborn-again cannot enter.

27:25.note: Six of John 3:7's eight words, in order, with the addressee replaced by a universal catalogue. The chapter's conversion narrative is Pauline and its conversion doctrine is Johannine, which is the division of labour this verse marks: Alma has just been knocked down like Saul and now explains what happened to him in the vocabulary of Nicodemus. Catalogued as a quotation because the borrowed frame is complete, though it is far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold (CONVENTIONS §2).
bibliography: Frederick 2016 — his index of co-occurrence (data/frederick-refs.json, from tools/parse-frederick.py) places Mosiah 27:25 within 1500 characters of his discussion of John 1:12-13; that index records proximity in his argument about the Gospel of John, not a proposed source.

27:25.text: And will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty.

provenance.other: “my sons and daughters” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 6:18. The phrase elsewhere in the KJV is always ‘thy sons and thy daughters’ or ‘your sons and your daughters’, addressed to parents about their children rather than by God about his people.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 6:18 is the KJV's one divine adoption formula in this exact form, and it closes a paragraph demanding separation from unbelievers — ‘come out from among them, and be ye separate’. Mosiah 27:25 uses it of people ‘changed from their carnal and fallen state’, and the chapter's opening problem was precisely a church surrounded by unbelievers it could not separate from. This is the third Corinthian borrowing in the chapter, after 27:5's two.

27:25.note: ‘Becoming his sons and daughters.’ A KJV singleton in the exact possessive Mosiah needs, and the only place English scripture lets God speak of a people as his sons and daughters. Moderate because the phrase is short and the idea of divine adoption has many KJV homes; what makes it worth a row is that this particular wording has only one.

27:26.text: Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.

provenance.other: “new creature” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, 2 Corinthians 5:17 and Galatians 6:15, both Pauline and both singular. Mosiah 27:26 pluralizes: ‘thus they become new creatures’.
provenance.significance: Both KJV occurrences make the new creature a description of a state — if any man be in Christ, he is one — and neither makes it a requirement. Mosiah 27:26 makes it one: ‘unless they do this, they can in no wise inherit the kingdom of God.’ Paired with John 3:5 in the same sentence, this is the chapter's move again: a New Testament indicative converted into a Book of Mormon condition, in the same way 26:21 converted John 10:27's description of sheep into a rule of admission.

27:26.note: The pluralized phrase and the kingdom-of-God consequence come from two different sources fused in one clause — Paul's new creature and John 3:5's kingdom no one enters unborn. Moderate: two words, but they are two words the KJV uses twice, and the fusion with John 3 is already established four verses earlier.

27:28.text: Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.

provenance.other: “much tribulation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 14:22. Tribulation is ‘great’ in Matthew 24:21 and Revelation, and it is ‘much’ only here.
provenance.significance: Acts 14:22 has three clauses and Mosiah 27 uses all three within eight verses, out of order but complete: the kingdom of God that must be entered (27:26, ‘can in no wise inherit the kingdom of God’), the much tribulation one passes through to reach it (27:28, ‘after wandering through much tribulation’; 27:32, ‘preaching the word of God in much tribulation’), and the confirming and exhorting of disciples (27:33, ‘confirming their faith, and exhorting them with long suffering’). The source verse describes Paul and Barnabas returning to congregations they had planted in cities that had stoned them; Mosiah 27:32-33 describes converts returning to a church they had persecuted, in cities where they are now smitten. The parallel is doing structural work, not decorative.

27:28.note: A KJV singleton phrase at 27:28, and the other two clauses of the same KJV verse at 27:26 and 27:33. One link rather than three, on the rule that a phrase adopted within a book is recorded in recurrenceRefs rather than re-argued (ADJUDICATING §4); but the distribution is the evidence here, because a writer borrowing only ‘much tribulation’ would not also have ‘kingdom of God’ two verses before it and ‘confirming … and exhorting’ five verses after it.

27:28.text: The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?

provenance.other: “everlasting burnings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 33:14, in the plural; Mosiah 27:28 has the singular, ‘an everlasting burning’. The snatching has its own KJV background in the firebrand ‘plucked out of the burning’ of Amos 4:11 and Zechariah 3:2.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 33:14 asks the question as an unanswerable one — who among us can live with everlasting burnings? — and its speakers are the sinners in Zion, frightened. Mosiah 27:28 answers it in the first person and in the past tense: one of the sinners in Zion has been snatched out. The verse the KJV leaves as a rhetorical question about the impossibility of survival is turned into a report of a survival, which is the whole rhetorical situation of Alma's speech.

27:28.note: ‘The Lord in mercy hath seen fit to snatch me out of an everlasting burning.’ The noun phrase exists once in the KJV and Mosiah has it singular; the verb is not Isaiah's, and the firebrand-plucked-from-the-burning idiom of Amos 4:11 and Zechariah 3:2 lies behind it. Moderate rather than high because the two elements come from different places and neither clause is reproduced.

27:29.text: For I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity.

provenance.other: “gall of bitterness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “bond of iniquity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse, Acts 8:23. The two phrases exist in English scripture only in each other's company, and Mosiah 27:29 has them in Acts's order, with ‘bonds’ pluralized.
provenance.significance: Acts 8:23 is Peter's sentence on Simon Magus, who tried to buy the power of the Holy Ghost — a man inside the church, baptized, who wanted its authority for himself. That is the diagnosis Alma applies to his own former state, and it is a sharper self-accusation than the chapter has otherwise made: Alma has been described as a persecutor, an idolater and a flatterer, but the phrase he chooses for himself is the one the KJV reserves for a baptized man who wanted the priesthood on his own terms. Simon's story ends unresolved — ‘Pray ye to the Lord for me’ — and Mosiah 27's ends with the prayers answered. The link supplies the outcome Acts 8 withholds.

27:29.note: Two KJV singletons from one verse, adjacent and in order. This is the chapter's most secure borrowing after Acts 9:4, and unlike that one it is not part of the Damascus material — it comes from four chapters earlier in Acts and from a very different kind of sinner. That Alma's self-description reaches past his own Saul-shaped conversion to Simon Magus is the finding worth keeping.

27:29.text: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light;

provenance.other: “marvellous light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 2:9, and the 1830 text spells it with the KJV's double l. The 1920 edition modernized it to ‘marvelous’, which is the spelling the current text carries.
provenance.significance: 1 Peter 2:9's darkness-to-light is said of a whole people and in the passive — you were called out. Mosiah 27:29 says it of one man and in the active present: ‘I was in the darkest abyss; but now I behold the marvellous light of God.’ The change from being called into light to beholding it is what makes the sentence a testimony rather than a doctrine, which is what the verse is for; and coming three verses after Alma has described himself as Simon Magus, it moves him from Acts 8 to 1 Peter 2 — from the man who wanted the priesthood illegitimately to the people who are one.

27:29.note: A KJV singleton, and one whose 1830 spelling is the KJV's own. This is a textbook case of CONVENTIONS §8: the first edition preserves an orthography that the modern text has erased, so the borrowing is fractionally more visible in the running text than in the book a reader owns. The 1830 also reads ‘My soul was wrecked with eternal torment’ where 1920 has ‘racked’ — not a KJV question, but worth noting alongside.

27:31.text: I have sworn by myself, the word is gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and shall not return, That unto me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.

provenance.route: Isaiah 45:23 → Romans 14:11 / Philippians 2:10-11 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “every knee shall bow” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Isaiah 45:23 and Romans 14:11. The word that separates the Old Testament form from the New is the second verb: Isaiah's tongue shall SWEAR, and both New Testament forms have it CONFESS (Romans 14:11 ‘every tongue shall confess to God’; Philippians 2:11 ‘every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord’). Mosiah 27:31 reads ‘every tongue confess before him’, and then twice more, ‘then shall they confess that he is God’.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's decidable mediation case and it decides cleanly on one word. The Book of Mormon has Isaiah's couplet with the New Testament's verb, so the route runs through Romans or Philippians rather than straight from Isaiah 45. Which of the two is the proximate witness cannot be settled: Romans 14:11 supplies the couplet's shape and Philippians 2:11 supplies the construction Mosiah actually uses twice in the next clause, ‘confess that he is God’ against ‘confess that Jesus Christ is Lord’. Philippians is marginally favoured on that construction, and Philippians 2:10-11's setting — the last-day acknowledgement by every creature, including the unwilling — is the setting Mosiah 27:31 builds out at length. Note that tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence for either New Testament witness, because Mosiah's clause diverges from both after the shared words; the swear/confess substitution has to be read by eye.

27:31.note: ‘Every knee shall bow, and every tongue confess before him.’ Isaiah's couplet with Paul's verb — the single substitution that distinguishes the New Testament citations of Isaiah 45:23 from Isaiah 45:23 itself. Mosiah then does what neither source does and extends the confession into a formal admission of the justice of one's own sentence, ‘that the judgment of an everlasting punishment is just upon them’, which is the chapter's characteristic turn of a doctrine into a procedure.

27:31.text: That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:

provenance.other: “without God in the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 2:12, where it is the last of four descriptions of the Gentiles' former condition.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 2:12's whole force is that it is past tense — ‘at that time ye were’ — and 2:13 immediately cancels it: ‘but now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh.’ Mosiah 27:31 uses the phrase for people whose condition is not cancelled: ‘then shall they confess, who live without God in the world, that the judgment of an everlasting punishment is just upon them.’ Alma is the man for whom Ephesians 2:13 has just happened — two verses earlier he was in the darkest abyss and now beholds the light — and he applies the uncancelled half of the same sentence to everyone else. The present tense ‘who live’ is doing all the work.

27:31.note: A five-word KJV singleton, unaltered. Its interest is entirely in the tense: Ephesians uses it of a past state that grace has ended, and Mosiah 27:31 of a present state that judgment will end differently. The link is high because the phrase is exact and unique; the argument is about what has been done to it.

27:37.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

provenance.route: Isaiah 52:7 → KJV → Mosiah 12:21 (Abinadi's transcription) → Mosiah 15:14-18 (his exposition) → Mosiah 27:37
provenance.other: “good tidings of good” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:7. Nahum 1:15 has the mountains, the feet, the good tidings and the published peace but not the doubled ‘good tidings of good’, and Romans 10:15, the New Testament citation, has neither: it reads ‘preach the gospel of peace’ and ‘glad tidings of good things’.
provenance.alternative: Romans 10:15, ruled out by tools/mediation-check.py and by the wording — Mosiah has Isaiah's verb (publish, not preach) and Isaiah's unique phrase (good tidings of good, not glad tidings of good things).
provenance.significance: Two mediation questions, and they answer in opposite directions. Against Romans 10:15 the verse is decisively Isaiah's, on the verb and on a KJV singleton. But it is not Isaiah's directly: Isaiah 52:7 has participles governed by a construct — him that publisheth peace, that bringeth good tidings of good — and Mosiah 27:37 has finite verbs with a plural subject, ‘they did publish peace; they did publish good tidings of good’. That conversion has already been performed in this same book, by Abinadi at Mosiah 15:14, ‘these are they which hath published peace, that hath brought good tidings of good’. So Mosiah 27:37 is following the Book of Mormon's own exposition of Isaiah rather than Isaiah, and it takes the conversion one step further by making both clauses use ‘publish’ where Isaiah and Mosiah 15 alike use ‘bringeth’ or ‘brought’ for the second. The chapter that began with a man destroying the church ends by giving him and his companions Isaiah's title for the messenger — and it gives it to them in the words the prophet he had grown up hearing about had already put it in.

27:37.note: ‘They did publish peace; they did publish good tidings of good; and they did declare unto the people that the Lord reigneth.’ Isaiah 52:7's three clauses in Isaiah's order, with the participles finite and the addressee changed from Zion to the people. The KJV singleton settles the source against Romans 10:15; the grammar settles the route through Mosiah 12:21 and 15:14, where Isaiah 52:7 is transcribed and then re-cast in exactly this way. Mediation is therefore OT-via-earlier-BoM rather than direct-OT.

27:23.text: And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.

provenance.other: “fasted and prayed” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Nehemiah 1:4 and Acts 13:3; only Acts 13:3 has the plural subject and the pluperfect Mosiah 27:23 has, ‘when they had fasted and prayed’.
provenance.significance: Acts 13:1-3 is the church at Antioch fasting and praying, laying hands on Barnabas and Saul, and sending them away — the commissioning of the persecutor-turned-preacher for his first journey. Mosiah 27:22-23 has the priests assemble, fast and pray, and Alma rise; 27:32-35 sends him and the four sons of Mosiah travelling round about through all the land. The source verse is the sending of Saul, which is the event Mosiah 27 has been reproducing since verse 10, and it arrives at the same point in the sequence: after the conversion, before the journey.

27:23.note: ‘After they had fasted and prayed for the space of two days and two nights.’ Five words of a two-verse KJV phrase, in the construction only Acts 13:3 has, at the point in a Damascus-shaped narrative where Acts 13 falls. Moderate: the phrase is short and the act is unremarkable, but the position in the sequence is not, and the chapter's dependence on Acts is established elsewhere at much higher confidence.
